# Diagnosing Intermittent Turn Signals on a 2002 Jeep Grand Cherokee Laredo

Intermittent electrical failures in older vehicles often stem from thermal expansion, corrosion, or loose connections rather than component failure in the traditional sense. When a 2002 Jeep Grand Cherokee Laredo's turn signals work for a few days and then cease entirely, replacing the flasher relay is frequently the first instinctive step. While this action addresses a known common point of failureâspecifically the high-resistance contacts within the relay that overheat when the bulb load is correctâit does not account for every scenario. If the relay replacement yields no permanent fix, you must systematically evaluate the signal path upstream and downstream to identify the actual break in continuity.

The multifunction switch (the stalk on the steering column) is a primary suspect, but it is rarely the sole cause of this specific symptom unless accompanied by other indicators like dimming hazard lights or erratic dashboard cluster behavior. In many Chrysler products from this era, the switch contains internal carbon brushes and resistive elements that degrade over time. When these contacts oxidize or become pitted, they create high resistance. Under normal operating conditions, the voltage drop might not be enough to stop the bulb from illuminating immediately. However, as the vehicle vibrates on rough roads or as temperatures fluctuate between day and night, the connection can physically separate or expand enough to break the circuit completely. This explains the "intermittent" nature of the failure: the signal works until the mechanical stress or thermal shift breaks the fragile contact.

Before committing to replacing the multifunction switch, which is a labor-intensive procedure requiring the removal of the steering column cover and potentially the airbag clockspring, you should verify the integrity of the wiring harness. The most likely culprit for an intermittent failure that mimics a bad switch is a loose ground or a cracked wire in the under-hood fuse box. Specifically, check the connection for the 40A turn signal fuse (often labeled "PWR DOOR" or similar depending on trim) and the dedicated ground point near the firewall. If the metal tab inside the fuse block is corroded or if the ground strap has loosened due to engine vibration, the circuit will open under load but may briefly complete again when the vehicle settles. This is a much simpler repair than replacing the switch.

If the wiring and grounds check out clean, then the multifunction switch becomes the definitive next step. Replacing this component involves removing the steering wheel (requiring a 12V battery disconnect to prevent airbag deployment), removing the column cover screws hidden under rubber grommets, and unbolting the switch assembly. Once removed, you can visually inspect the internal terminals for white oxidation or carbon buildup. If corrosion is present, cleaning the contacts with contact cleaner may extend the life of the original unit temporarily, though replacement is often more cost-effective given the age of the vehicle.

It is also worth noting that this specific symptomâturn signals failing while hazard lights might still function differentlyâis a classic signature of internal switch resistance. The hazard mode bypasses some of the internal resistive paths used for left/right indication, which is why the problem might not manifest immediately after ignition but appears under specific load conditions. If you have verified the ground, the fuse integrity, and the relay, swapping the multifunction switch is the logical conclusion to restore full functionality to the vehicle's lighting system.
